approachQuestion.prompt: W03 — Fewest transfers in a network. You are given an undirected network as adjacency lists, a starting station s, and a destination t. Return the minimum number of links between them, or -1 if no route exists. Example 1: A:[B,D], B:[A,C], C:[B,D], D:[A,C], start=A, destination=C returns 2 (V=4, E=4). Example 2: A:[B], B:[A], C:[], start=A, destination=C returns -1 (V=3, E=1). V is the number of vertices and E is the number of undirected edges; each edge appears in both endpoint lists. Which method guarantees the fewest links for every such input?
constraints: The graph is undirected and unweighted; every link has a cost of exactly one transfer.
The adjacency lists are already built; do not count them as additional algorithm space.
Each vertex has a unique identifier; s and t are vertices in the graph.
1 <= V <= 1,000,000; no adjacency list contains duplicate neighbors or self-loops; the result (-1 or a transfer count) fits in a signed 32-bit integer.
Each queue insertion and removal takes constant time; visited and distance lookups take expected constant time.
W03 is a Premium problem and is not eligible for the Free pool.

options.text: Run breadth-first search from s. Record each vertex’s distance when it is first discovered, then read the distance to t.
options.feedback: Layer-by-layer discovery sets a vertex’s distance when it is first reached, so that distance is minimal.

options.text: Return the length of the first path to t found by depth-first search.
options.feedback: A depth-first search does not visit vertices by distance layers. Counterexample: A:[D,B], B:[A,E,C], C:[B], D:[A,E], E:[D,B]; every edge appears at both endpoints. Start=A, destination=C. Process each vertex’s neighbors in the listed order. The search follows A-D-E-B-C first, a route with 4 links, even though A-B-C has only 2.

options.text: Run Dijkstra’s algorithm with a min-heap, assigning weight 1 to every edge.
options.feedback: The result is correct for every allowed input, but a priority heap and priority updates add unnecessary work when every edge has the same cost.

options.text: Run breadth-first search from t and read the distance to s.
options.feedback: In an undirected graph, a route has the same length in either direction. Starting from the destination is equally optimal.

feedback.reason: Distinguish layer-by-layer exploration from an arbitrary traversal, while using the fact that all links have equal cost.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Choose the time and additional-space pair for bfs-from-start. V is the number of vertices and E is the number of undirected edges (each appears in two adjacency lists). Queue operations take constant time; visited and distance lookups take expected constant time. Exclude the input adjacency lists and the single-value output from additional space. Include the queue, visited set, and distance table.
constraints: Use the worst case; do not assume the destination is found early.
Mark each vertex as visited when it is enqueued, so it enters the queue at most once.

options.text: O(V + E) time, O(V) additional space
O((V + E) log V) time, O(V) additional space

feedback.reason: Each vertex is enqueued at most once, and each adjacency entry is scanned once. There are 2E adjacency entries in total. The visited set, queue, and distance table each hold at most a constant number of values per vertex.

methodReveal.title: Breadth-first layers from the start
methodReveal.description: Put the start station in a first-in, first-out queue with distance zero. Remove stations from the front of the queue. When a station is first discovered, mark it visited as you enqueue it and assign a distance one greater than its predecessor. After all stations at distance k have been processed, newly discovered stations have distance k+1. The first assigned distance for the destination is minimal. If the reachable part of the graph is exhausted first, return -1.
